title: Body odor as an emotional marker: Experimental validation of aggression-associated chemosignals in emotion research
summary: In this study, participants are asked to donate body odor under controlled conditions. After a screening and adhering to certain behavioral rules (e.g., no alcohol, no spicy foods), they shower with odor-neutral products and wear special cotton shirts with underarm pads. Odor samples are collected in two situations: after a neutral condition and after a provocative condition designed to specifically trigger anger and frustration. Additionally, self-assessments, scientifically proven questionnaires, saliva samples for hormone measurements (cortisol and testosterone), biochemical analyses of sweat (VOCs), and physiological reactions such as heart rate and skin conductance are collected. The aim of the study is to investigate whether and how emotional states change—and whether these changes are also reflected in body odor. The collected odor samples will be used in a subsequent study (DRKS00035762) to investigate their effects on other people. The present study also aims to demonstrate whether this method can be used to reliably generate odor stimuli suitable for further scientific experiments.
conditions: Healthy control subjects, exclusion criteria: female, regular medication use, regular drug use, regular smoking, age under 18 or over 50 years, non-compliance with the prescribed behavioral rules for odor control (e.g., consumption of alcohol, spicy foods, garlic, or asparagus before the odor donation)

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Male gender
Age between 18 and 50 years
Healthy physical and mental condition (self-reported)
Non-smoker
No medication or drug use
Willingness to adhere to odor-related behavioral rules, in particular:
Avoidance of alcohol, spicy foods, garlic, and asparagus
Use of odorless hygiene products before donation
Consent to all planned procedures (questionnaires, saliva samples, physiological measurements, odor collection)
Exclusion criteria:
Female gender
Regular use of any medication
Regular drug use
Smoking
Age under 18 or over 50 years
Failure to comply with odor-related behavioral guidelines
Refusal to consent to key study procedures (e.g., odor collection, hormonal or physiological measurements)
